title: Wall Street Has No Idea What Anthropic Is Worth
dek: Anthropic sets its IPO range and Wall Street promptly argues about whether it's too high, too low, or a referendum on the whole AI trade, while a new Claude productivity suite knocks Microsoft's stock. Meanwhile Google's Gemini 4 Carbon finally ships, Nvidia's spy scandal deepens, and OpenAI posts a record quarter. The honest takeaway from all the IPO numbers: nobody actually knows yet.

oneIdea.headline: Heading into Anthropic's IPO, we know a lot of numbers and almost nothing at all.
oneIdea.summary: Anthropic is pricing at $70–78 a share, implying $1.25–1.4 trillion, and its banks are already mulling a bump to $1.5 trillion on strong demand. Bears read the drift down from the splashy $2 trillion chatter as a warning for the AI trade. Contrarians point to $81 billion in run-rate revenue and retail desperate for frontier-lab exposure. The valuation targets were never Anthropic's own; they came from anonymous investors and stuck. Microsoft dipping on a Claude spreadsheet launch is more evidence of a market flailing until the stock actually trades. Buckle up: the next phase starts next week.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Supplier durability is the practical question
items.body: Most of this edition is about share prices, which do not touch clinical work. The link to us is that scribes and other NHS tools are built on models from a handful of labs. NLW reads the flotation as a company raising cash it needs and investors unsure how to value it. Zitron reads the same filing as a firm whose fixed bills demand flawless growth. Neither view changes what we do tomorrow, but both support the same habit: ask a supplier which model it depends on, whether it could switch, and what the contract says about price rises.

items.title: Cheaper models, seen from both sides
items.body: Google's new model came within one bug of the leader on a coding test at under a quarter of the cost. For a buyer that is good news, and it should feed through to what scribe vendors charge. Zitron's point is the mirror image: Anthropic's own filing shows discounts and price cuts took about $600 million off one quarter's revenue. Falling prices help the NHS now and strain the suppliers. Short contracts and fixed prices suit that position better than long commitments.

items.title: Staff building their own tools
items.body: Anthropic says its lawyers, who do not write code, built a review tool that cut a three-day turnaround to a day. A practice manager could do something similar for rotas or recall lists. The NHS runs on Microsoft and that will not change soon. The caution is governance: anything touching patient data needs a data protection impact assessment and, if it informs care, clinical safety sign-off.

the_other_side.text: Zitron, writing eight days earlier on the amended filing, treats the falling valuation not as noise but as one sign among several that the money is running out. He argues Anthropic has committed to about $447.5 billion of compute spending before the end of 2030, expects a junk credit rating, and will have to borrow at eight to eleven per cent to cover the gap. He says its obligations are "priced for perfection", requiring it to double in a year, while Ramp expects fourth-quarter growth of only 15 to 25 per cent. He also claims around four fifths of its revenue comes from venture-backed startups, so growth depends on venture capital continuing to flow.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether Anthropic's revenue can keep growing faster than the fixed compute bills it has signed. Both accept the filed numbers: a price range implying about $1.25 to $1.4 trillion, run-rate revenue in the tens of billions, and several hundred billion dollars of commitments falling due by 2030. The empirical question is whether growth holds once those payments start. The observables are the first public quarterly results, fourth-quarter growth against Ramp's forecast of 15 to 25 per cent, and the interest rate on any debt Anthropic raises. The residue is worldview: whether demand for AI labour is durable, or on loan from venture capital. For Whittemore to be vindicated, revenue must broaden beyond coding into finance, law and life sciences, and the shares must hold. For Zitron, growth must stall while costs rise and lenders balk. Both are polemicists with incentives, Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both say today's figures cannot tell you what this company is worth. Watch the first day of trading next week.

headlines.headline: Gemini 4 Carbon finally ships, and it lives up to the preview
headlines.summary: Google previewed Carbon at the end of October as the top model on the Artificial Analysis Index but held it back for the government's voluntary safety testing. Two weeks later, Fable 5.2 has taken the top spot, but early testers are finding lots to like. Ethan Mollick: it shows "Google is back in the race of frontier models, rapid releases, and rapid improvement."

headlines.headline: Carbon nearly matches the leader on coding at under a quarter of the cost
headlines.summary: On Pavel Hurin's bug-hunt test, Carbon found 57 of 105 bugs, one behind Fable 5.2's 58, and completed the run for $31 versus almost $140. The cost savings held across other use cases: one render test matched Fable 5.2 at a third of the cost. One tester: "Nobody should be laughing at Google anymore."

headlines.headline: Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month's time.
headlines.attribution: Pushmeet Kohli, VP at DeepMind, on Carbon's formal verification of Signal
headlines.summary: DeepMind showcased Carbon formally verifying Signal's security properties, which required analyzing the underlying machine code. Formal verification is usually dismissed as too complex and time-consuming to be practical. Kohli pitched the result as frontier AI acting as a force multiplier against modern cyber threats.

headlines.headline: Trump defends Jensen as the Nvidia spy scandal spreads
headlines.summary: At a Monday press conference, President Trump said the FBI is looking into the matter but called Jensen Huang "a very honorable man." He acknowledged knowing about the affair before it was reported but was vague on timing. The New York Times reported he was fully briefed last April and chose to do nothing.

headlines.headline: Up to $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips may have flowed to China via Megaspeed
headlines.summary: Sources who claim to know the alleged spy, Alice Huang, told The Information that a vast smuggling network sat behind Megaspeed, the Neocloud that employed her. They gave a full recap of how the chips flowed through it.

headlines.headline: A Commerce probe into Megaspeed reportedly stalled after Nvidia got in touch
headlines.summary: Per The New York Times, Nvidia's general counsel discussed the case directly with investigators, saying their superior had approved the contact. Agents worried that was "potentially tainting the case." Commerce is now working on new export controls, including closing the remote-access loophole, but is delaying an entity-list decision on Megaspeed. House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast says he'll subpoena Jensen if he won't come in.

headlines.headline: Nvidia has no succession plan, and that boxes in its own board
headlines.summary: Jensen runs a famously flat company with 60 direct reports. The Wall Street Journal reports there is no succession plan and a board treated more as a governance formality than a check on the CEO. With an outside law firm investigating, removing a charismatic CEO with no successor looks risky even if the findings are damning. The Journal suggests a "reined-in" Jensen is the best option.

headlines.headline: The whole country now carries Nvidia's keyman risk
headlines.summary: Nvidia is down 11% since the story broke and makes up about 7% of the S&P 500 and 8% of the Nasdaq, so most US investors are heavily exposed. Its success is also now a national-security matter because of the AI race. There is no simple fix. NLW: the entire nation is experiencing "the mother of all keyman risks."

headlines.headline: OpenAI posts a record $10B+ quarter and finally gets a growth story back
headlines.summary: Q3 revenue rose 50% from Q2, after Q2 growth of only 17% compared with Anthropic's 144%. The drivers were API demand for recent models, including GPT-6 Astra, quietly strong image-model demand, and ads running at a $1 billion annualized pace. Operating losses grew to an estimated $10.1–10.9 billion, though operating margin improved from −150% to −109%.

headlines.headline: OpenAI acquires an AI travel agent built the AI-first way
headlines.summary: The startup, founded less than a year ago by Sonder founder Francis Davidson, booked $60 million in travel across tens of thousands of users last summer. Davidson says he threw out the old playbook for a lean, AI-first process, including dictating about 1.2 million words a month. The service has shut down, and OpenAI is quiet about its travel plans.

headlines.headline: ChatGPT's business agents turn ads into conversations
headlines.summary: OpenAI's new business hub gives advertisers an analytics-style dashboard and lets brands deploy "business agents" that consumers can talk to after clicking an ad. NLW reads this as the start of ChatGPT competing more directly with Meta. Expect much more treatment of ChatGPT as a commerce platform, since so many of its answers already touch shopping.

headlines.headline: The blue wave didn't stop it: Anthropic goes public before Thanksgiving
headlines.summary: Some speculated that the midterm wave bringing data-center opponents to power might deter Anthropic. Instead it has kicked off its roadshow and is aiming to list next week.

headlines.headline: Anthropic's messaging finally clicks: miracles first, risks second
headlines.summary: Nothing in Dario's roadshow pitch, an "age of miracles" with risks carefully addressed, is new. What's new is the balance. The miracles are the point, and the risks are what must be overcome to get there. That ordering has eluded the company in the past.

headlines.headline: Of course I do. I'm a patriot.
headlines.attribution: Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, to Bloomberg's Emily Chang
headlines.summary: Emily Chang asked whether he was comfortable with Claude helping the military kill more people more quickly. Dario reframed it as whether he wants a stronger country, then said decisions about military use aren't the technology provider's to make beyond some very high-level boundaries. After the clashes with the Department of Defense/War, NLW notes he has never been quite this crisp.

headlines.headline: The numbers: $70–78 a share, $1.25–1.4 trillion, about $100 billion floated
headlines.summary: Anthropic seeks to raise $57–64 billion in the IPO, plus $26 billion from industry partners Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and Broadcom, with Nvidia and Google in for up to $10 billion each. With the greenshoe option, the total float comes to around $100 billion.

headlines.headline: Anthropic never "settled" for less than $2 trillion
headlines.summary: The $2 trillion figure came from an anonymous investor source of unknown proximity to the company, and it was splashy enough to stick. Anthropic couldn't respond during its quiet period. The slide from $2T to $1.6T to $1.5T to talk of $1.1T says something about shifting investor mood, but it isn't a goal Anthropic set and missed.

headlines.headline: Within a day, the range already looked too low
headlines.summary: The Financial Times reports Anthropic's bankers plan to raise the share price to a top-end valuation of $1.5 trillion after "strong indications of demand." The FT adds that Anthropic cares far more about raising cash than about valuation, given its large compute commitments.

headlines.headline: The real lesson of the price debate: nobody knows
headlines.summary: Investors have no clear idea what to expect, what's reasonable, or what other investors think is reasonable. Bears say the lower valuation is bearish and that a weak debut will trigger another leg down in the AI trade. Until the stock trades, everyone is flailing.

headlines.headline: The contrarian case: $81B run rate and retail starving for exposure
headlines.summary: Artemis's John Ma says the consensus view is now bearish: overvalued, revenue flattening, tokens commoditizing. The counter: run-rate revenue rose $10 billion in October alone to $81 billion, still driven mainly by coding agents. Finance, legal, and life sciences are barely tapped, and retail investors may pile in regardless and push it toward $3 trillion.

headlines.headline: At $1.4 trillion, Anthropic is priced like CrowdStrike, not Palantir
headlines.summary: iCapital's Sonali Basak notes that $1.4 trillion is around 40× trailing 12-month revenue. Palantir trades at roughly 55×, which puts Anthropic closer to the multiples of CrowdStrike and Cloudflare.

headlines.headline: The bigger compute risk may sit with the Neoclouds
headlines.summary: Anthropic disclosed $10 billion in new seven-year commitments with Microsoft and Google. It also said its $35 billion Lambda deal is cancelable after Lambda missed a deadline, though it doesn't currently intend to cancel. That reframes the worry about hundreds of billions in non-cancellable commitments: which fails first, AI demand or Neoclouds' ability to finance and deliver data centers on time?

headlines.headline: Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data take aim at Microsoft's turf
headlines.summary: Claude Sheets is an Excel competitor built for collaboration between humans and agents. Whiteboards is a team planning surface. Claude Data, which evolved from Dashboards, pulls live CRM and database feeds and competes with Power BI, with model-generated visual data stories and narrated videos added on top.

headlines.headline: Anthropic's lawyers cut marketing reviews from three days to 24 hours
headlines.summary: Anthropic framed the suite as where work is heading, not a declaration of war. Its legal team built a Slack-based review tool that drafts redlines from its own playbook. Its finance team turned an executive update into an interactive page the team maintains with Claude. Neither team writes code.

headlines.headline: The fight over where work happens started in November 2022
headlines.summary: Once Claude becomes the shared work surface, it needs this kind of infrastructure around it. The place where work happens is increasingly inside the LLM harness or app, and this suite is a natural extension of that. Matthew Berman: "If you build software, the labs will compete with you." Microsoft fell 2.2% on the news.

headlines.headline: Microsoft is investor, landlord, reseller, and now competitor
headlines.summary: The counterpoint: no enterprise is ditching Excel, and Claude Sheets even exports to it. Microsoft is buying into the IPO, is owed $45 billion in cloud spend, and resells Claude through Copilot. NLW sees the dip as more evidence of a market still working out what this all means.
